analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Drugs is a commodity API manufacturer with no discernible pricing power — operating margins of 6.16% and ROCE of 13.1% are below my 15% minimum hurdle, and the business has been shrinking in real terms since its 2021 COVID windfall. At 16.8x P/E on declining earnings with heavy ongoing capex consuming nearly all operating cash flow, this is a fair price for a fair-to-poor business.
key_strengths: Low leverage (D/E 0.39, finance costs stable ~INR 39 Cr) limits downside risk in a tough cycle
Promoter at 55% ownership signals alignment; DII at 10% provides institutional floor
Diversified API portfolio across NSAIDs, fluoroquinolones, antidiabetics — not dependent on a single molecule
key_risks: Margins structurally under pressure: EBITDA contracted from INR 490 Cr (2021) to INR 307 Cr (2025) despite 11% higher revenue vs 2020 — the pricing power simply doesn't exist
FCF is nearly absent: cumulative FCF 2022–2025 is only INR 87 Cr while capex consumed INR 720 Cr — capital is being deployed with poor incremental returns
Revenue is declining (INR 2,716 Cr in 2023 → INR 2,387 Cr in 2025), suggesting the 2021 peak was a COVID-era anomaly, not durable earnings power
red_flags: EBITDA CAGR of only 3.9% over 9 years vs revenue CAGR of 8.6% — a classic margin destruction story in a commoditized business
Net profit in FY25 (INR 168 Cr) is barely above FY20 (INR 141 Cr) despite 32% higher revenues — zero operating leverage over five years
Cash balance at INR 5 Cr against total debt of INR 615 Cr — the balance sheet offers no cushion if the API cycle worsens further
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Invert first: what would make this a bad investment? A commodity manufacturer with thin 6% operating margins, no pricing power, ROIC below 15%, and a business that peaked in 2021 on COVID tailwinds — that is precisely what Aarti Drugs is today. The 2021 results (INR 280 Cr net profit, INR 490 Cr EBITDA) were a one-time anomaly driven by API demand spikes, not a reflection of the business's normalized earning power. Since then, every key profit metric has contracted: EBITDA is down 37%, net profit down 40%, and operating margins have compressed to 6.16%. This is not a business that earns its cost of capital over a cycle.

The capital allocation record reinforces the concern. Management has spent INR 720 Cr in capex over four years (FY22–25) while generating only INR 87 Cr in cumulative free cash flow — a deeply negative spread. CWIP ballooned to INR 261 Cr in FY24, indicating ambitious expansion, yet ROIC remains stuck at ~13%. At 16.8x P/E and 13.2x EV/EBITDA on contracting earnings, the market is not pricing in the cyclical risk adequately. There are far better API businesses in India — companies with ROIC above 20% and genuine product differentiation — that deserve capital before this one does.
